method: The complete eight canonical interlinear discourses Chanukah 9–16 were read in order. Each listed paragraph was then compared with the explicitly named, actually read candidates from both schools, using complete target paragraphs and necessary surrounding context. The entries record finite editorial decisions, not an exhaustive claim about every possible parallel. Retrieval rankings and matching quotations did not establish relevance. Hebrew and canonical annotation text were preserved; translated excerpts and directional explanations were reviewed separately. No reverse direction is approved in this batch.

entries.assessment: Read the complete opening in the seven-paragraph ois, including the restriction of festival status to Hallel and thanksgiving and the Levush/Taz problem answered in 9:2. Approved two different explanatory contributions: how recurrence was recognized, and what praise changes in perception. Neither establishes a feast or a work prohibition.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: the returning light in the following year explains the permanent establishment, and praise has the stated inward task of removing evil. The full target paragraph, including its Beit Shammai conclusion, was read.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Sod Yesharim, Shabbat Chol HaMoed Sukkot 36:1

Not approved at this anchor: the Modim/serpent discussion and the distinction between patriarchal qualities do not explain the act of making these days festive.

entries.assessment: Read all arguments: bodily rescue, toil in Oral Torah, second tablets and Yom Kippur, Solomon’s table versus acquired spiritual nourishment, and the concluding Chanukah application. The shared anchor is the second-tablet joy amid fasting; the explanations preserve the different laws of Chanukah and Yom Kippur. The larger Yisrael canonical paragraph includes inherited internal headings; the selected exact excerpt avoids them.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: the voluntary approach, fasting, and acquisition of Oral Torah explain the inward meaning of the second tablets. Full canonical paragraph read, including the later contrast with Purim and the holy sparks discussion.

Approved: the five afflictions allow reception of the spiritual nourishment not yet clothed in bodily food. The target’s full rebuilding, integrated qualities, and garment argument were read; no Chanukah fast is inferred.
Not selected here: its bread/feast distinction includes the unfinished condition of collective joy, but the more exact new contribution concerns Jacob and his descendants at 10:3.

entries.assessment: Read the entire paragraph: Hallel as Torah of kindness, patriarchal opening blessings, twelve tribes, Joseph’s division, and the additional blessing against division. Approved the exact account of why each tribe corresponds to a petition. The Ishbitz candidates do not explain that mapping closely enough.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: each tribe has a distinct excellence and lack; the twelve petitions gather those needs into dependence on God. The full paragraph’s contrast between prayer in deficiency and offerings in fullness was read.
Not selected at this anchor: its fellowship and threefold intellectual structure illuminate the threefold cord at 11:1, but not the twelvefold petitions.

Sod Simchat Torah 1:2 has an inherited attribution of Birkat HaZan to Joshua later in the paragraph; that wording is outside the selected quotation and is not repeated as accurate bibliography.

Not selected here: its interior establishment of mitzvot is substantive, but does not explain the blessing on food as directly as the selected Simchat Torah passage.

The Tiferet comparison explicitly does not replace the origin’s separate prayer counsel for someone unable to attain Torah learning.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: the illuminated Torah itself is the divine assistance named in the shared Talmudic statement. Full target read, including its later treatment of human authorship and attribution to God.

entries.assessment: Read both the annual dedication/compensation argument and the full Modim explanation. The canonical origin names Rabbi Meir; primary Yerushalmi Berakhot 2:4, 17b (https://mechon-mamre.org/b/r/r1102.htm) attributes the spontaneous bow to Rabbi Matanya. English marks this inherited attribution correction explicitly; Hebrew and pins remain unchanged. The selected anchor preserves the distinction between an individual soul’s answered prayer and communal redemption still unfulfilled. Both targets explain spontaneous bowing through an established inward relation, rather than using the visible gesture as automatic evidence of perfection.

Not repeated: the enduring inherited root already has its proper argument and quotation at 11:3.

The different geometry in Sod Shemini Atzeret was not forced into an agreement.
